content: The degree of heterogeneity among studies included in a comparison was evaluated using the I² statistic. When studies only reported odds ratios with confidence intervals, the data were combined using the generic inverse variance method. For analyses involving adjusted results (e.g., regression modeling), a sub-analysis was conducted using only the adjusted data. Funnel plots were employed to assess the presence of reporting bias. The strength of evidence was evaluated using the GRADE methodology, and a GRADE assessment was generated for each meta-analysis and sub-analysis. For populations such as mental health or substance use patients living with hepatitis C, no downgrading for indirectness was applied, as recommendations from this analysis were deemed relevant to these specific populations. Comparisons most pertinent to current viral hepatitis treatment guidelines were included in the results section, while other comparisons were detailed in supplementary materials. A total of 11,806 titles were identified through database searches, with an additional 19 titles identified via reference searches and author contact. After removing duplicates, 7,581 titles were screened based on standard inclusion and exclusion criteria. Of these, 469 abstracts were selected for further screening, and 353 were excluded. Following abstract screening, 116 articles were selected for full-text review, ultimately resulting in the inclusion of 54 studies in this systematic review. These included 45 full-text publications, 5 abstracts, and 4 clinical trials. Of the 54 studies, 31 were included in a meta-analysis that calculated a pooled effect size. Among the 54 included studies, 37 reported outcomes along the hepatitis C virus (HCV) care continuum, 15 reported outcomes along the hepatitis B virus (HBV) care continuum, and 2 studies reported outcomes involving both HBV and HCV. Interventions to improve retention along the HBV care continuum were limited to screening and linkage to care, whereas interventions for the HCV care continuum addressed all five steps. The most commonly reported outcomes were HCV treatment adherence (including treatment completion) and HCV viral suppression, reported in 21 and 20 studies, respectively. HBV and HCV screening outcomes were reported in 15 and 11 studies, respectively. HBV and HCV linkage to care and treatment uptake were less frequently studied. None of the interventions aimed at improving HBV or HCV screening specifically targeted symptomatic or asymptomatic individuals. Thirty percent (30/54) of the included studies were non-randomized studies (NRS), with sample sizes ranging from 21 to 36,987 participants. Thirteen meta-analyses were conducted where studies were deemed sufficiently similar in terms of intervention, control, and outcome to allow pooling of data. The number of studies included in each meta-analysis ranged from two to six. The limited number of studies in each comparison precluded stratified analyses for risk of bias, intervention intensity, and other relevant factors. Funnel plots did not detect reporting bias in any of the 13 meta-analyses. Nearly half (7/15) of the interventions to improve HBV screening involved lay health worker (LHW)-led HBV test promotion activities. Six of these seven LHW-led interventions were one-time activities delivering culturally tailored educational content to specific communities, primarily targeting Asian communities in the United States or Canada. Results from these six studies were pooled in a meta-analysis, which found that LHW-led interventions had a positive effect on HBV screening, though the results were moderately heterogeneous (I² = 56%). This heterogeneity may be attributed to differences in study design (three were cluster-randomized controlled trials [RCTs], and three were individually randomized RCTs) and intervention settings (three involved home visits, and three were delivered at community-based organizations). All three studies examining clinician reminders to prompt HCV screening during clinical visits found a positive effect on HCV screening rates. However, there was significant heterogeneity in the reported effect sizes (I² = 99%). All three studies involved patients seeing primary care providers in New York City clinics. The heterogeneity in effect sizes may be partially explained by differences in the intensity of interventions, which included varying degrees of patient education, case management, and facilitated referral. In some contexts, HCV-positive patients were deemed ineligible for HCV treatment due to ongoing mental health and/or substance use comorbidities. Interventions in these cases involved regular contact between mental health and specialist treatment providers, as well as the provision of psychological therapy and counseling for patients with these comorbidities. Some interventions also included varying levels of patient education and case management before and during treatment. Despite differences in additional services provided, patient genotypes, and percentages of patients with comorbidities, little heterogeneity in effect size was observed for treatment adherence and viral suppression outcomes. Meta-analyses for interventions to improve HBV screening included culturally tailored LHW educational sessions aimed at improving HBV knowledge and promoting testing. These sessions were compared to no education or unrelated educational sessions. All six studies included in this meta-analysis were at high risk of detection bias because the outcome (self-reported HBV screening) was assessed six months post-intervention. Although all studies involved Asian immigrants in North America, this was not considered a significant enough difference to downgrade the evidence, as the intervention strategies were not exclusive to this population. The confidence interval was not wide, and the pooled sample size exceeded the optimal information size (OIS). However, three of the six included studies were cluster RCTs, none of which accounted for clustering in their analyses, leading to a unit-of-analysis error and over-precise results. No intraclass correlation coefficients (ICCs) were reported, preventing statistical methods from reducing the effective sample size of the cluster RCTs. Despite this limitation, proper adjustment for cluster design was unlikely to significantly impact the precision of the pooled results. Meta-analyses for interventions to improve HCV screening included clinician reminders to prompt HCV screening during clinical visits, with or without supplementary provider education. This meta-analysis included one cluster RCT and two NRS. One study was at high risk of performance bias and did not adjust for confounding introduced by its non-randomized design. Another study did not report the comparability of randomized clusters, placing it at high risk of bias. The high degree of heterogeneity (I² = 99%) may be due to differences in HCV screening algorithms used in each intervention. Although the pooled sample size exceeded the calculated OIS, the confidence interval was wide. Additionally, the cluster RCT did not account for clustering in its analysis, leading to a unit-of-analysis error and over-precise results. No ICC was reported, preventing statistical methods from reducing the effective sample size of the cluster RCT. The pooled results were not upgraded for large effect due to the significant possibility of confounding introduced by the non-randomized design of two of the three studies. Meta-analyses for interventions to improve HCV linkage to care included facilitated referral and scheduling to specialist visits by staff at the site of established care, with or without supplementary HCV education and post-test counseling. One study relied on self-reported HCV status and attendance at specialist visits, placing it at high risk of detection bias. However, this study's small sample size did not place the entire meta-analysis at high risk of bias. The high degree of heterogeneity (I² = 85%) may be due to differences in the intensity of interventions across studies. The confidence interval was not wide, and the pooled sample size exceeded the OIS. Meta-analyses for interventions to improve HCV treatment initiation included coordinated care between mental health and treatment specialists, with psychological therapy and counseling for patients with mental health and/or substance use comorbidities. One RCT and two NRS were included. The high degree of heterogeneity (I² = 77%) may be due to differences in the populations under investigation and the interventions provided. The confidence interval was not wide, but the pooled sample size did not meet the OIS threshold. Meta-analyses for interventions to improve HCV sustained virological response (SVR) included coordinated care between mental health and treatment specialists, with psychological therapy and counseling. One study was at high risk of performance bias due to differences in treatment received by the two cohorts beyond the intervention under examination. Another study did not adjust for confounding introduced by its non-randomized design. The confidence interval was not wide, and the pooled sample size exceeded the OIS. This systematic review and meta-analysis demonstrated that operational interventions can improve engagement, retention, or progression through the chronic viral hepatitis care continuum. Specifically, LHW-led HBV screening promotion activities increased HBV test uptake, while clinician reminders to prompt HCV screening during clinical visits increased HCV testing rates. Coordinated care between hepatitis and mental health specialists, along with psychological therapy and counseling, improved treatment initiation and outcomes for patients with mental health and/or substance use comorbidities.
